snip.t:
❏ It is the same as ARDS except that it is caused by a deficiency of
pulmonary surfactants in new borns, most often as a result of
immaturity.

Alveolar‑capillary membrane – thin type I pneumocytes for gas exchange, type II cells produce surfactant: Infection fills alveoli with exudate → loss of surfactant → atelectasis and impaired O₂ diffusion, producing hypoxaemia and dyspnoea.

Alveolar walls (type I & II pneumocytes, interstitium): Necrosis of type I cells produces a cavity; loss of type II cells impairs surfactant, promoting atelectasis and further hypoxia that favours anaerobes.

Pulmonary surfactant system – type II pneumocytes produce phospholipid film: Damage or loss of type II cells reduces surfactant → alveolar collapse (atelectasis) and contributes to stiff lungs; also releases profibrotic cytokines (e.g., TGF‑β).

Pulmonary surfactant system – type II pneumocytes produce phospholipid film: Toxic gases (chlorine, ammonia) denature surfactant → alveolar collapse, acute respiratory distress, and later fibrosis if exposure persists.

Toxic gases (chlorine, ammonia) → direct epithelial injury → loss of surfactant → alveolar collapse → acute inflammatory exudate → chemical pneumonitis → possible progression to fibrosis if repeated exposure.

Alveolar type I & II cells – type I for gas exchange, type II produce surfactant and act as progenitors.: Peripheral adenocarcinomas often arise from type II cells or bronchioalveolar stem cells; loss of surfactant regulation contributes to tumour‑induced inflammation.
Children with surfactant protein B deficiency have a very good prognosis

qs.q: Which specific alveolar wall cell type synthesizes surfactant and serves a vital regenerative role following epithelial injury?
o: Type I pneumocytes forming the barrier
qs.e: Type II pneumocytes are rounded cells responsible for surfactant synthesis and alveolar repair after type I cell damage. Type I pneumocytes primarily form the thin plate-like barrier for gas diffusion.

qs.q: How should surfactant therapy be administered to a neonate with respiratory distress syndrome?
o: Instilled directly into the lungs via a tracheal tube or fine catheter
Administered intravenously as a continuous infusion over several hours
Given orally in divided doses mixed thoroughly with infant formula milk
Delivered topically via an inhaled nebulizer mask placed on the face
qs.e: Surfactant therapy is given by instilling surfactant directly into the lungs via a tracheal tube or a fine catheter inserted between the vocal cords. Intravenous or oral routes are ineffective for delivering surfactant to the alveolar surface.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which meconium causes diffuse atelectasis through surfactant impairment?
o: Free fatty acids strip surfactant from the alveolar surface due to high surface tension.
Bile salts directly destroy type II pneumocytes located within the pulmonary alveoli.
Cellular debris physically blocks the natural production of lamellar bodies.
Mucus and lanugo form a dense waterproof barrier over the alveolar membrane.
qs.e: Free fatty acids in meconium have a higher minimal surface tension than surfactant and strip it from the alveolar surface. This deactivates and inhibits surfactant, resulting in diffuse atelectasis.

qs.q: Which specific cellular component is responsible for synthesizing the components of pulmonary surfactant?
qs.e: Pulmonary surfactant components are synthesized in the Golgi apparatus of the endoplasmic reticulum of type II alveolar cells. Mitochondria are not the primary site of this synthesis.

qs.q: What is the functionally principal phospholipid that makes up the majority of pulmonary surfactant?
qs.e: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, also known as lecithin, is functionally the principal phospholipid of surfactant. Phosphatidylglycerol serves as a marker for lung maturity but is not the primary functional phospholipid.

qs.q: An infant is diagnosed with respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency. Which physiological change directly contributes to right-to-left shunting?
o: Increased lung compliance and residual capacity
qs.e: Impaired surfactant synthesis leads to atelectasis, V/Q inequality, and hypoventilation, resulting in large V/Q mismatches and right-to-left shunts. Lung compliance and functional residual capacity are actually decreased, not increased, in this condition.

qs.q: When should intratracheal surfactant be administered to a neonate with respiratory distress syndrome who requires assisted ventilation?
o: Only after 72 hours of life when healing begins
When inspired oxygen exceeds 0.40, ideally within 2 hours
Exclusively when mechanical ventilation fails after 1 week
Prior to birth via direct intra-amniotic injection
qs.e: Neonates requiring assisted ventilation with an FIO2 greater than 0.40 should receive intratracheal surfactant as soon as possible, preferably within 2 hours after birth. Waiting 72 hours would miss the critical early therapeutic window.

qs.q: How many doses of surfactant do most neonates with respiratory distress syndrome typically require?
qs.e: Most neonates with respiratory distress syndrome require 2 doses of surfactant therapy. Rapid improvement after a single dose suggests respiratory distress syndrome is unlikely.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, keeping lungs open and preventing collapse. It is produced by type II pneumocytes and is crucial for breathing, especially in preterm infants.

sections.p: Surfactant is a phospholipid-protein complex secreted by type II alveolar cells. It coats the alveolar surface, lowering surface tension and allowing the lungs to expand with minimal effort.
By reducing surface tension, surfactant prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) during exhalation and stabilises the lung volume throughout the breathing cycle.
Surfactant synthesis is up‑regulated by glucocorticoids and by the maturation of type II cells. In preterm infants, surfactant production is insufficient until about 34–36 weeks.
Deficiency or dysfunction leads to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm infants and can cause acute respiratory failure in adults with ARDS.

t.b: Detects B-lines indicating interstitial fluid; helps differentiate RDS from other causes of respiratory distress
Low compliance suggests surfactant deficiency; guides need for exogenous surfactant

sections.p: Exogenous surfactant therapy is lifesaving for preterm infants with RDS. In adults, surfactant dysfunction contributes to ARDS severity and mortality.
b: Surfactant replacement reduces mortality in preterm RDS

t.b: PaO2/FiO2 ratio <200 indicates ARDS severity; surfactant therapy considered in severe cases
Ground‑glass opacities suggest surfactant dysfunction in ARDS

sections.p: Remember that surfactant is a phospholipid-protein complex secreted by type II cells; its deficiency causes RDS in preterms and contributes to ARDS in adults. Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so it is contraindicated for pneumonia.

whenToSeekHelp: Respiratory distress in a newborn <34 weeks gestation
Severe hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 <200) in adults with ARDS

faq.q: Why is surfactant therapy given to preterm infants?
faq.a: It replaces the insufficient endogenous surfactant, preventing alveolar collapse and improving oxygenation.

faq.q: What causes surfactant deficiency in adults?
faq.a: Severe lung injury, infection, or inflammation (e.g., ARDS) damages type II cells or inactivates surfactant.

faq.q: Can surfactant be used for pneumonia?
faq.a: No; surfactant inactivates daptomycin, and exogenous surfactant has no proven benefit in bacterial pneumonia.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of respiratory distress syndrome in a 28‑week preterm infant.
Describe how surfactant deficiency contributes to the clinical picture of ARDS.
Outline the indications and contraindications for exogenous surfactant therapy.
